questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{4i}}}={e}^{\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{4i}}}={e}^{-\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{4i}}+B{x}^{-\text{4i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

questions.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-4,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+20{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+20{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +20] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-2\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-2+4\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{-2-4\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{-\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{-2+4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-2-4\text{i}} \\  & =A\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}+B\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(x)$ as follows:

$$
y(x)=\frac{{c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-4.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=2$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{2[(4+{c}_{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(2-2{c}_{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)]}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =-2[2-2{c}_{2}] \\ -4 & =-4+4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.
$$
